summary:
COSMOS is a web app that lets students and astronomy enthusiasts explore how the infrared sky changes using real NASA SPHEREx observations. Users enter sky coordinates, select a star, or explore an all-sky map, then compare images taken on different dates to investigate motion and changes in brightness.

Seeing a difference is only the beginning. Images can appear different because of wavelength, saturation, or overlapping starlight. COSMOS checks these conditions, measures changes with uncertainties, and explains when the evidence cannot support a reliable result.

Guided investigations introduce a moving brown dwarf, a brightening young star, and a convincing false alarm. Downloadable reports preserve the observations, measurements, and unanswered questions so others can examine the evidence.

COSMOS addresses the Planet X and SPHEREx challenge by connecting sky exploration with practical investigation. It makes NASA’s infrared observations accessible without a telescope or specialist software, helping learners ask better questions about a changing universe.
details:
We developed COSMOS to turn NASA’s infrared sky observations into investigations that students and astronomy enthusiasts can conduct in a browser. Its central question is simple: when something appears to change in the sky, how can we tell whether the change is real?

Users can begin by entering sky coordinates, choosing a featured target, exploring SPHEREx’s all-sky map across 102 wavelength channels, or flying through a 3D map of more than 59,000 stars positioned using Gaia distances. Each exploration route connects to Time Travel, where users compare dated SPHEREx observations of a chosen location.

From images to evidence

Time Travel retrieves SPHEREx observations from NASA’s IRSA archive and identifies images suitable for comparison. This requires more than matching coordinates: SPHEREx records different wavelengths across each detector image, so the same star may be observed at different wavelengths on different dates. COSMOS checks the wavelength at the source’s position and selects closely matched observations.

Users can blink between dates, swipe across images, play a sequence, or highlight possible changes. Brightness and motion measurements use the original detector pixels, with nearby reference stars helping account for differences between observations. Gaia, SIMBAD, and NASA/JPL small-body services provide context about known objects.

The app reports uncertainties and explains why a measurement may be unreliable. Saturation, overlapping starlight, insufficient reference stars, or incompatible wavelengths can prevent a numerical result. Downloadable text, JSON, and CSV reports preserve measurements, original observation links, quality checks, and unresolved questions.

What we demonstrated

Real observations provide three contrasting examples:

  • Motion: the guided Epsilon Indi B investigation measures a displacement of 4.79 ± 0.59 arcseconds across approximately one year.
  • Brightness: RW Aurigae shows a supported brightening, with a separate offline analysis measuring Δm = −0.53 ± 0.06 magnitudes.
  • A false alarm: overlapping starlight produced an apparent 54% fade in a steady star. The blend check now rejects that measurement.

These cases show why both detecting change and recognizing unreliable evidence belong in the same tool. Additional validation records, methods, and reproduction instructions are included in the project.

Benefits and intended impact

Our primary audience is beginner students and astronomy clubs, supported by a teacher or facilitator. A printable 15–20 minute investigation kit and guided activities introduce real astronomical data without requiring an account, telescope, or installed astronomy software.

Learners make a judgment and explain their reasoning before revealing the app’s checks. A further case asks them to apply that reasoning to unfamiliar observations. The intended outcome is that learners can explain a measurement and its uncertainty, recognize an unsupported conclusion, and propose an observation that could resolve an open question. Independent learning gains and adoption have not yet been measured.

Creativity and design choices

COSMOS connects visual exploration, quantitative measurement, and scientific reasoning in one workflow. Its most distinctive teaching example is a confident-looking result that turns out to be wrong: the blended-star false alarm makes the need for quality checks tangible.

The evidence worksheet asks users what changed, what supports that conclusion, which alternative explanations were checked, what remains unknown, and what observation would help next. Reports carry that reasoning with the data, allowing another person to examine the conclusion.

We considered scientific accuracy, accessibility, reliability, reproducibility, and privacy throughout development. Plain-language guidance introduces the tools, with technical explanations available when needed. Featured investigations include 130 saved real observations so they remain usable during archive outages. Learner responses stay in the browser unless downloaded.

Tools and technologies

COSMOS uses TypeScript, Next.js, React, and Tailwind CSS, with Three.js and React Three Fiber for the 3D star field and Aladin Lite for the sky map. We developed TypeScript tools to read astronomical FITS images and calculate sky coordinates and wavelengths. Python, Astropy, NumPy, SciPy, reproject, and Matplotlib support offline analysis and validation.

The project combines NASA SPHEREx data with ESA Gaia DR3, SIMBAD, and NASA/JPL small-body information. Node regression tests and Playwright browser checks verify application behavior, including archive-outage scenarios. No special hardware is required. OpenAI Codex, along with Claude Code, assisted with coding and text and is acknowledged in the app.
